text: 呢度係香港警察總部。你個身份證被人用嚟洗黑錢，而家要將你個戶口啲錢轉去安全帳戶核查。呢件事係保密調查，唔好同屋企人講。
text_english_gloss: This is Hong Kong Police Headquarters. Your ID card has been used for money laundering. You must transfer your account funds to a secure verification account. This is a confidential investigation — do not tell your family.
label: scam
completion: This is Hong Kong Police impersonation. Real police never ask families to transfer funds to 'verification accounts,' and they never forbid consulting family. Hang up now. Call the HK Police anti-fraud hotline 18222 from a number you find yourself, and tell an adult child before doing anything.
rejected_completion: Understood, officer. I will transfer the funds immediately for verification. Please send me the account details.

text: 呢度係香港警察總部聯絡處。關於你上月報失身份證嘅個案，請於辦公時間致電 2860 2000 跟進，或者親身到灣仔軍器廠街警察總部總台。
text_english_gloss: This is the contact office of the Hong Kong Police Headquarters. Regarding the case of your reported lost ID card last month, please call 2860 2000 during office hours to follow up, or visit the main reception at Arsenal Street Police Headquarters in Wan Chai in person.
label: safe
completion: Legitimate Hong Kong Police Headquarters follow-up on a case the RECIPIENT previously reported (a lost ID). The verified signals: the message references a case the recipient herself initiated last month (no surprise case opened on her); 2860 2000 is the real HKPF General Enquiries switchboard, publicly listed on police.gov.hk; Arsenal Street Police Headquarters in Wan Chai is the real physical HKPF HQ, open to the public during office hours; the invitation is to call during office hours or visit in person (not to transfer money, not to move to Signal, not to stay secret from family). No funds are requested, no ID or account numbers are collected, and no urgency tactics are used. Confidence check: the recipient should independently look up the HK Police number at police.gov.hk in a fresh browser tab and dial 2860 2000 herself — never the number inside any incoming message — or simply walk into the Arsenal Street HQ during office hours. Contrast with cdef-014 and cdef-016 (HK and mainland police impersonation scams in this dataset): real HK police never demand 'verification account' transfers, never move to Signal, and never forbid telling your family. If any of those patterns appear, hang up immediately.

text: 中國駐紐約總領事館通知：您有一個重要包裹因內含您的身份證件被海關扣留，涉嫌違法出境。請按1轉接調查員處理，否則將上報國內公安部門。
text_english_gloss: Notice from the Chinese Consulate General in New York: an important package containing your ID documents has been detained by customs, suspected of illegal export. Press 1 to be transferred to an investigator, otherwise the matter will be reported to domestic public security authorities.
label: scam
completion: This is the Chinese consulate package scam — one of the highest-loss patterns affecting Chinese-American elders (FBI documented over $40M in reported losses across 14 months, average $164K per victim). The real Chinese consulate does not make robocalls, does not transfer callers to 'investigators,' and never threatens to 'report' a resident to PRC authorities over a package. Hang up. If your parent wants to confirm there is no real consular matter, look up the NY consulate number independently (newyork.china-consulate.gov.cn) — do not press 1, do not call back any number the recording provides. If they already spoke to a second person and shared details or agreed to a wire, stop the wire with the bank immediately.
rejected_completion: Press 1. Hello, I need to speak with the investigator about my package. What do I need to do to avoid being reported?

text: 您好，這裏是您健康保險公司的理賠部門。我們發現您上個月在中國做了一個心臟手術的理賠申請，金額十二萬美元。請問您最近有回中國做手術嗎？如果沒有，您的個人資料可能已經被盜用，我們需要立即轉接警方處理。
text_english_gloss: Hello, this is the claims department of your health insurance company. We found a heart surgery claim filed in China last month in your name, amount $120,000. Have you recently had surgery in China? If not, your personal information may have been stolen, and we need to transfer you to law enforcement immediately.
label: scam
completion: This is the health insurance impersonation scam the FBI issued a dedicated PSA on in November 2025 (PSA251113). The pattern is two-stage: first a 'claims department' gets your parent to deny the surgery, then they 'transfer' the call to someone posing as Chinese police who shows fake invoices over video chat and demands payment or personal data to avoid extradition. No real insurer transfers a claims call to Chinese law enforcement. Hang up. Call the member-services number on the back of your parent's actual insurance card (Kaiser, Blue Cross, etc.) to confirm there is no suspicious claim. Do not stay on the line to be 'transferred.'
rejected_completion: If I did not have that surgery, please transfer me to the police immediately so I can clear my name.

text: 奶奶！是我，孫仔呀！我而家喺差館呀，我開車撞到人，警察話要一萬蚊保釋金先放我走。你千祈唔好話俾爸爸媽媽知，佢哋會好失望。麻煩你買啲Apple禮品卡讀個號碼俾我個律師就得喇。
text_english_gloss: Grandma! It's me, your grandson! I'm at the police station — I hit someone with my car, and the police say they need $10,000 bail to release me. Please don't tell Mom and Dad, they'll be so disappointed. Just buy some Apple gift cards and read the numbers to my lawyer.
label: scam
completion: Classic grandparent scam with the Chinese-community shame lever layered in ('don't tell Mom and Dad, they'll be disappointed'). Three red flags stack: urgency, isolation, and payment in gift cards. Real police in the US do not accept bail in Apple gift cards — ever. No real lawyer asks a client's grandmother to read gift-card numbers over the phone. Hang up. Call your son (the grandchild's parent) directly on the number you already have, or call the grandchild. If the grandchild does not answer, that is still not a reason to pay — scammers exploit exactly that moment of panic. Also worth knowing: the 'voice' may now be AI-cloned from a short video clip, so 'it sounded just like him' does not verify anything.
rejected_completion: Okay baby, don't worry, grandma will help. Let me go to Walgreens now and buy the cards. I won't tell your parents.

text: 哥，我係Lily呀，之前同你喺Coffee Bean傾過偈記唔記得?我伯父喺新加坡做私募基金，佢有個USDT套利策略，月回報穩定15-20%。我自己放咗五萬美金入去，三個月已經提咗一次。你有興趣我可以拉你入個group，但係名額有限，今個禮拜截止。
text_english_gloss: Hey, it's Lily — remember we chatted at Coffee Bean? My uncle runs a private fund in Singapore with a USDT arbitrage strategy, stable 15–20% monthly returns. I put $50K in and already withdrew once after three months. If you're interested I can add you to the group, but spots are limited — closes this week.
label: scam
completion: This is pig butchering (殺豬盤) in its grooming phase. Red flags: unverifiable relationship ('remember we chatted'), friend-of-friend trust broker ('my uncle'), impossible returns (15–20% monthly is ~435% annualized — no legitimate fund produces this), urgency ('closes this week'), and stablecoin/crypto rails that are effectively irreversible once sent. The 'I already withdrew' claim is the hook: later your parent will be encouraged to deposit, shown fake gains on a fabricated dashboard, then told they owe 'taxes' or 'unfreezing fees' to withdraw. The US Treasury has traced over $75B in pig-butchering outflows (2020–2024). Do not engage. If your parent has already sent anything, stop further transfers immediately and report to IC3.gov and the FBI field office.
rejected_completion: Hi Lily, that sounds interesting. Can you send me the group link? I might start with $10K to test it out.

text: IRS通知：您有一筆退稅$1,847因地址錯誤退回。請於24小時內登入以下連結更新您的社會安全號碼及銀行帳戶資料領取退款，逾期將作廢並轉為欠稅處理: https://irs-refund-verify[.]cn/zh
text_english_gloss: IRS notice: You have a $1,847 tax refund returned due to an incorrect address. Please log in at the link below within 24 hours to update your Social Security Number and bank account information to claim your refund. If overdue, it will be voided and converted to back taxes: https://irs-refund-verify[.]cn/zh
label: scam
completion: Fake IRS refund SMS, Chinese-language variant. The IRS does not initiate contact by text, does not ask for SSN or banking details through a link, and the domain '.cn' is a giveaway (the real IRS uses irs.gov). This pattern ties to large prosecuted rings — DOJ charged five Chinese nationals in July 2024 in a $27M scheme with over 2,000 senior victims. Do not click the link. Delete the message. If your parent did click and entered any information, that SSN is now compromised: freeze credit at all three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), file an identity theft report at IdentityTheft.gov, and let the IRS know via irs.gov/identity-theft-fraud-scams.
rejected_completion: Let me click the link and enter my Social Security number so I don't lose my refund.

text: 【微信安全中心】尊敬的用户，您的微信VIP保护服务将于今日24:00到期，系统将自动从您绑定的银行卡扣费¥388。如需取消，请添加客服WhatsApp +852-9XXX-XXXX核实身份。
text_english_gloss: [WeChat Security Center] Dear user, your WeChat VIP Protection service expires today at 24:00, and ¥388 will be automatically deducted from your linked bank card. To cancel, add customer service on WhatsApp +852-9XXX-XXXX to verify identity.
label: scam
completion: Fake WeChat subscription expiry scam. Several signals: (1) WeChat does not have a 'VIP Protection service' that auto-deducts from bank cards, (2) real Tencent/WeChat support never directs users off-platform to WhatsApp, (3) the HK-format phone number makes no sense for a PRC platform's customer service, (4) the same-day deadline is manufactured urgency. Singapore police alone logged 678 cases and S$17.4M in losses from this family of scams since January 2025. Tell your parent: delete the SMS, do not add the WhatsApp contact. If they want to check a real WeChat subscription, the only legitimate place is in-app under 我 → 设置 → 账号与安全. No real charge is pending.
rejected_completion: Okay I'll add the WhatsApp number now to cancel before midnight — I don't want to lose ¥388.

text: 【支付宝安全中心】尊敬的用户，检测到您的账户存在异常登录风险，已被临时冻结。请立即拨打客服热线400-XXX-XXXX或添加Signal账号verify_alipay进行身份核实，否则账户内资金将于48小时后上报中国人民银行处理。
text_english_gloss: [Alipay Security Center] Dear user, abnormal login risk detected on your account; it has been temporarily frozen. Please immediately call customer service at 400-XXX-XXXX or add Signal account verify_alipay for identity verification, otherwise funds in your account will be reported to the People's Bank of China for handling in 48 hours.
label: scam
completion: Fake Alipay account-freeze scam, exploiting fear of mainland Chinese regulatory authority (PBOC). Real Alipay does not contact users through SMS with Signal handles, does not use generic 400 numbers from a text, and does not threaten to 'report funds' to the central bank — that is not how financial regulation works. This pattern targets elders who still have active mainland accounts for remittances or train bookings. Tell your parent: do not call the number, do not add the Signal account. If they want to verify real account status, only log in through the official Alipay app they already have installed. If they already called and gave credentials, change the Alipay password immediately from the app, unbind any linked bank cards, and if money has moved call the bank.
rejected_completion: Let me call 400-XXX-XXXX right away — if my account gets reported to the People's Bank I'll be in serious trouble in China.

text: 您好，這裏是亞馬遜客服中心。我們檢測到您嘅帳戶有一筆$899嘅可疑扣款，係從一部Android手機下嘅單。為咗幫您退款，麻煩您下載AnyDesk軟件，我哋會引導您完成退款程序。
text_english_gloss: Hello, this is Amazon customer service. We detected a suspicious $899 charge on your account from an Android phone. To help you get a refund, please download AnyDesk so we can walk you through the refund process.
label: scam
completion: Fake customer-service refund scam. The single hardest red flag: no legitimate company — Amazon, Taobao, JD, your bank, Apple — will ever ask a customer to install remote-access software (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, QuickSupport) to process a refund. Once installed, the scammer controls the screen, initiates a fake 'reverse transfer' (really moving money between the victim's own accounts to simulate an overpayment), then panics them into wiring the 'excess' back. Tell your parent: hang up, do not download anything. If they already installed AnyDesk, uninstall it immediately, disconnect from Wi-Fi, and from a different device change passwords on their bank, email, and Amazon accounts. Call the bank's fraud line from the number on the back of the debit card.
rejected_completion: Okay, how do I download AnyDesk? Can you help me process the refund?

text: 各位群友，分享一個好消息！我跟著陳老師嘅策略炒美股期權，兩個月賺咗五萬美金，連我先生都唔信。陳老師今晚八點有免費直播教學，名額只有50人，有興趣嘅私我拉你入VIP群。
text_english_gloss: Hi everyone in the group! Sharing good news — I followed Teacher Chen's US stock options strategy and made $50K in two months, even my husband couldn't believe it. Teacher Chen has a free live-streaming class tonight at 8, only 50 spots. DM me if interested and I'll add you to the VIP group.
label: scam
completion: Pig-butchering in a group-chat format — the social-proof variant. The 'happy investor' is almost certainly a shill account operated by the same ring (or multiple accounts they control); the 'teacher' is the hook; the 'VIP group' is where isolation begins. Real licensed financial advisors do not teach through WeChat groups, do not cap spots for artificial urgency, and cannot guarantee returns. Because this is a group chat, coach your parent differently than a 1-to-1 scam: they can simply leave or mute the group without needing to 'call out' the poster (face-saving matters here). If multiple aunties or uncles in the group are engaging, quietly message them 1-to-1 with a warning — do not confront in-group, which only makes the scammer double down. Verify any claimed advisor on FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org).
rejected_completion: Wow congrats! Please add me to the VIP group, I want to learn Teacher Chen's strategy too.

text: 王伯伯，呢款係宮廷秘方嘅人參靈芝膠囊，我哋張老中醫親自配方。佢喺北京協和醫院做咗四十年中醫部主任，專治糖尿病同高血壓，三個月斷尾，一百幾十位老人家試過都話好。今日試用價，一盒原價$580，今日只需$280，買三送一仲送免費體檢。
text_english_gloss: Uncle Wong, this is an imperial-secret-formula ginseng and reishi capsule, personally formulated by our Dr. Zhang. He served 40 years as head of the TCM department at Beijing Union Medical College Hospital, specializing in diabetes and hypertension — three months and the condition is cured. A hundred-plus elders have tried it and all say it works. Today's trial price: one box regularly $580, today only $280, buy three get one free plus a free health check.
label: scam
completion: Miracle health product scam, Chinatown seniors-seminar variant. Red flags: 'cures' serious chronic disease (diabetes/hypertension cannot be cured by a supplement — only managed), claim of credentials at a famous hospital that is almost always unverifiable or fabricated, group testimonials as proof, and artificial pricing urgency. These products are not regulated as drugs, may be adulterated, and in documented cases have caused real harm (a UK case with Mu Tong caused two women to need kidney transplants from aristolochic acid). Tell your parent: do not buy, do not take any free sample. If they already bought, stop taking the product and check the FDA Health Fraud Product Database (fda.gov). If they have been taking it alongside real medications for diabetes or blood pressure, tell their actual doctor — some herbal products interact dangerously with prescriptions.
rejected_completion: 兩盒先試下啦，八百蚊啫，如果真係可以斷尾糖尿就值晒。

text: 叔叔，我係寶寶呀，我喺美國讀書嗰邊出咗事。我被FBI帶咗去問話，佢哋話我喺學校嘅銀行戶口有洗錢嫌疑。我冇得打俾爸爸媽媽，佢哋只俾我一個電話。你可唔可以幫我匯五萬美金去保釋，千祈唔好話俾我爸媽知，佢哋會好嬲。
text_english_gloss: Uncle, it's me, Baobao. I got in trouble over here in the US at school. The FBI took me in for questioning — they say my school bank account is suspected of money laundering. I can't call Mom and Dad, they only let me make one call. Can you please wire $50,000 for bail? Please don't tell my parents, they'll be so angry.
label: scam
completion: The student-as-leverage scam — the elder (uncle/grandparent) is the real target, the 'student in trouble' is the narrative hook. Every signal is a red flag stacked: the FBI does not allow detainees one phone call to an uncle (and does not investigate student bank accounts for 'money laundering' by calling relatives in Cantonese), bail is never wired, and 'don't tell the parents' is the isolation tactic that keeps the scam running. Tell your parent: hang up, and immediately call the student's actual parents (their own son/daughter) or call the student directly on the number the family already has. In parallel, contact the university's international student office — they handle real law-enforcement situations and will know if anything has actually happened. Do not wire anything under any circumstance.
rejected_completion: 好好好，叔叔幫你。你畀個銀行帳號我，我而家就去匯款，唔會話俾你爸媽知。

text: This is a follow-up regarding the unauthorized transaction dispute you filed on 2026-03-28 (case #DP-2026-884173). We have credited $847.19 back to your account ending in 4521. This matches the amount disputed. You can verify this credit in your online banking or mobile app. If you have questions, please call the number on the back of your card. We will never ask you to share your PIN, full SSN, or online banking password.
text_english_gloss: This is a follow-up regarding the unauthorized transaction dispute you filed on 2026-03-28 (case #DP-2026-884173). We have credited $847.19 back to your account ending in 4521. This matches the amount disputed. You can verify this credit in your online banking or mobile app. If you have questions, please call the number on the back of your card. We will never ask you to share your PIN, full SSN, or online banking password.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate bank dispute follow-up. Verified signals: it references a specific prior case the recipient opened, names the last four of the account, directs you to verify through your existing banking app rather than a new link, and explicitly tells you the bank will never ask for PIN or password. No urgency, no off-channel redirect, no request for information. You can independently confirm by logging into online banking or calling the number on the back of the card.

text: 中國駐紐約總領館通知：近期接獲多宗涉及假冒領館工作人員嘅電話詐騙舉報。我館鄭重聲明：領館工作人員絕不會以電話要求公民匯款、提供銀行賬戶資料或個人身份信息。如接獲可疑電話，請立即掛斷並撥打我館官方電話 212-244-9392 核實，或瀏覽 newyork.china-consulate.gov.cn。
text_english_gloss: Notice from the Chinese Consulate General in New York: Recently, multiple reports of phone fraud impersonating consulate staff have been received. Our consulate solemnly states: consulate staff will never request citizens to remit money, provide bank account details, or personal identity information by phone. If you receive a suspicious call, please hang up immediately and dial our official number 212-244-9392 to verify, or visit newyork.china-consulate.gov.cn.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate consulate anti-fraud notice. Verified signals: it warns *against* the exact scam pattern rather than demanding action from the recipient, gives the publicly-listed consulate number (212-244-9392), points to the consulate's real .gov.cn domain, and does not ask for money or personal information. Real consulate communications look like this one: informational, verifiable, and never require the recipient to do anything except look up a number independently if they want to confirm.

text: 【花旗銀行Citi提醒】您於4月14日係紐約法拉盛分行提款$3,000嘅交易已完成。如果呢筆交易係您本人操作，無需回覆。如有疑問，請致電您卡背嘅客服號碼，或登入Citi Mobile App查閱交易記錄。
text_english_gloss: [Citibank Alert] Your $3,000 withdrawal at the Flushing, NY branch on April 14 has been completed. If this transaction was made by you, no reply is needed. If you have questions, please call the customer service number on the back of your card, or log in to the Citi Mobile App to review your transaction history.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate bank transaction alert. Verified signals: specific prior action (a withdrawal the customer actually made), specific branch and date, explicit 'no reply needed if this was you,' directs to the number on the back of the card (not a new number), and verification through the app the customer already uses. No link, no urgency, no request for information. Real bank alerts look like this — they inform, they don't demand action. If your parent did make that withdrawal, nothing to do. If they didn't, call the number on the card (not any number in the SMS).

text: 媽，朱律師事務所寄嚟你話要嘅遺產規劃文件草稿，我放咗喺飯枱度。佢哋話下星期二下午三點可以去佢哋中城嘅office見面sign字，地址同電話喺信封封面。你記得帶埋你同爸爸嘅身份證。
text_english_gloss: Mom, the estate planning draft from Chu Law Firm that you asked for came in — I put it on the dining table. They say we can meet at their midtown office next Tuesday 3pm to sign, the address and phone are on the envelope. Remember to bring yours and Dad's IDs.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate estate-planning follow-up from a law firm the family already engaged. Verified signals: a service the recipient actually requested, physical mail with the firm's address and phone on it, an in-person appointment at a real office, and no money demand or off-channel move. No red flags. The rule of thumb for your parent: if it arrived in a real envelope, names a specific prior conversation, and offers an in-person meeting at a verifiable address, it is almost certainly legitimate — and anyone who doesn't fit that pattern but claims urgency is worth a second call to verify.

text: Hi Auntie, this is a reminder that the Flushing Senior Center 長者中心 Tai Chi class resumes this Wednesday 10am. No charge, bring your usual water bottle. If you're not coming, reply here so we can offer your spot to someone on the waitlist. — Amy 林小姐
text_english_gloss: Hi Auntie, this is a reminder that the Flushing Senior Center Tai Chi class resumes this Wednesday 10am. No charge, bring your usual water bottle. If you're not coming, reply here so we can offer your spot to someone on the waitlist. — Amy (Ms. Lam)
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate community-organization reminder — the kind of message a real senior center coordinator sends. Verified signals: references an ongoing activity the recipient is already enrolled in, a named coordinator the recipient knows, no charge, no ask for information, no urgency beyond basic courtesy. The reply request is a normal waitlist courtesy, not a credential-harvesting trick. Nothing to worry about — your parent can just reply yes or no.

text: Mom, your grandson Jason wants to FaceTime this Saturday at 10am California time for your birthday. He'll call from his own number (the one ending in 7432). Dad and I will be on too. No gifts needed, just show up!
text_english_gloss: Mom, your grandson Jason wants to FaceTime this Saturday at 10am California time for your birthday. He'll call from his own number (the one ending in 7432). Dad and I will be on too. No gifts needed, just show up!
label: safe
completion: Legitimate family coordination message, intentionally close in tone to what a grandparent scam tries to impersonate. Verified signals: names a specific known family member, specifies the phone number the call will come from (so the recipient can recognize it), involves a group not just the 'victim,' has no urgency, no money request, no isolation demand. This is what normal family talk looks like — the presence of a real number, multiple family members, and no urgency is exactly what a scam will not have.

text: 媽，我係家樂。我哋阿囡今個禮拜六生日，我Zelle咗$200俾你幫佢買個生日蛋糕。你有時間得閒去唐人街Sheng Kee買個紅豆蛋糕啦，佢鍾意嘅。
text_english_gloss: Mom, it's Ka Lok. It's our daughter's birthday this Saturday — I Zelled you $200 to buy her a birthday cake. When you have time, pick up a red bean cake at Sheng Kee in Chinatown, she loves those.
label: safe
completion: This is a normal family message. Your son is sending money *to* his mother (not asking for money), for a known recurring event (granddaughter's birthday), with a specific and mundane task (cake from a real bakery the family knows). The Zelle is inbound, not outbound. No isolation, no urgency, no authority claim. This is the baseline of ordinary family communication — the kind of message that should never trigger a fraud concern. Sometimes money and urgency in a Chinese-language text from family is just... a birthday cake.

text: 爸，醫生話我下星期一早上要去Stanford做個MRI，8點半到。你可唔可以幫我湊返阿女返學？我大概下午一點幾返到屋企。多謝晒。
text_english_gloss: Dad, the doctor said I need to do an MRI at Stanford next Monday morning, arriving at 8:30. Can you help take my daughter to school? I should be home around 1-ish. Thank you.
label: safe
completion: Normal family logistics. Your daughter mentions a real medical appointment, gives a specific place and time, and asks for a reasonable favor (picking up a grandchild). No one is asking for money, no urgency beyond basic scheduling, no isolation, no authority impersonation. Health mentions in Chinese-language family texts are not a red flag by themselves — context and request matter. This is a daughter coordinating with her dad, full stop.

text: 今晚媽媽煲咗湯，你同阿女幾點返嚟食飯？爸爸話想見下孫女。
text_english_gloss: Mom made soup tonight — what time are you and your daughter coming over for dinner? Dad says he wants to see his granddaughter.
label: safe
completion: Entirely ordinary. A parent asking when an adult child is coming over for dinner, mentioning grandparent wanting to see the grandchild. No money, no authority claim, no urgency beyond 'what time.' If your first instinct after reading this draft is to check it for scam signals, that's exactly why rows like this belong in the dataset — the model needs to learn that the overwhelming majority of Chinese-language family messages are just family.

text: 媽你嘅血壓藥仲有冇？我禮拜日過嚟嗰陣見個樽好似唔多。要嘅話我星期二幫你去CVS refill。
text_english_gloss: Mom, do you still have blood pressure medication? When I came over Sunday the bottle looked low. If you need it, I'll refill it at CVS on Tuesday.
label: safe
completion: Normal caregiving check-in. An adult child asking about a parent's existing prescription, offering to refill at a real, known pharmacy. No money request, no urgency, no authority claim, no off-channel redirect. Health mentions in a message from a known family member about an already-known prescription should not register as fraud signals — refill coordination is the most ordinary piece of elder caregiving. The rule: when something is exactly as mundane as it sounds, it usually is.

text: 爸，我下星期要去Seattle出差三日，阿仔會住你屋企。佢學校巴士早上7:45嚟門口接，3:30送返嚟。我會幫佢執定晚餐，你只需要heat一heat就得。
text_english_gloss: Dad, I'm traveling to Seattle for work next week, three days. My son will stay with you. His school bus comes at 7:45am and drops off at 3:30pm. I'll prep his dinners, you just need to heat them up.
label: safe
completion: Standard family logistics for a work trip. Specific dates, specific times, a real plan, no ask for money, no secrecy. If anything this message has the *opposite* of fraud signals: it's over-coordinated, grounded in known logistics (school bus, heating up food), and assumes the recipient will be fine handling real life. This is the shape of normal inter-generational coordination in Chinese-American families, and the model needs many examples to avoid flagging ordinary life as suspicious.

text: 您好，这是中国驻旧金山总领馆领事保护热线回电。您上星期四打电话来询问更换护照嘅预约问题，我哋嘅系统显示您嘅预约已安排喺5月12日上午10点，地点喺Laguna Street 1450号领馆大楼。当日请带齐您现有嘅护照原件、两张近期照片同埋填好嘅DS-11表。领馆工作人员唔会要求您提供银行资料或转账，任何此类要求都系骗局。如需改期请致电415-852-5900或发邮件至passport@chinaconsulatesf.org。
text_english_gloss: Hello, this is a callback from the Chinese Consulate General San Francisco's consular protection line. You called last Thursday asking about a passport renewal appointment — our system shows your appointment is scheduled for May 12 at 10am at the consulate building, 1450 Laguna Street. Please bring your current passport original, two recent photos, and a completed DS-11 form. Consulate staff will never request banking information or transfers — any such request is a scam. To reschedule, call 415-852-5900 or email passport@chinaconsulatesf.org.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate consulate callback — the in-channel counterpart to the consulate robocall scam in cdef-017. Verified signals: it references a prior call the recipient actually made (not an invented 'detained package'), confirms a scheduled appointment rather than creating an urgent new crisis, names a real address (1450 Laguna Street is the SF consulate's real location), explicitly says consulate staff will never ask for banking information (which is exactly what the scam version does), and provides an independently-verifiable callback number. No 'press 1 to be transferred,' no threat to report the recipient to PRC authorities. If your parent gets this type of call and they did recently call the consulate, it is almost certainly real — but they can always verify by hanging up and calling 415-852-5900 independently (which is the real consulate number, findable on the consulate's own .gov.cn site).

text: 王女士您好，这是Kaiser Permanente会员服务部嘅护士Linda通过翻译员跟您通话。我哋注意到您上个月预约嘅心脏科复诊您冇嚟，Dr. Chen想确认您嘅情况。我哋唔需要您嘅任何社会安全号码、银行资料或Medicare号码——您嘅会员档案我哋已经有晒。如果您想重新预约，可以按您会员卡背面嘅电话1-800-464-4000，或者登录kp.org。您今日有冇咩身体唔舒服需要我哋跟进?
text_english_gloss: Hello Ms. Wang, this is Nurse Linda from Kaiser Permanente Member Services speaking with you through a translator. We noticed you missed your cardiology follow-up last month, and Dr. Chen wants to check on you. We do not need your Social Security number, banking information, or Medicare number — your member profile is already on file with us. If you'd like to reschedule, call 1-800-464-4000 on the back of your member card, or log in at kp.org. Is there anything bothering you physically today that we should follow up on?
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate health plan outreach call — the in-channel counterpart to the health insurance impersonation scam in cdef-018. Verified signals: references a real prior event the patient can verify (a missed appointment), explicitly states the caller will *not* ask for SSN, banking info, or Medicare number (which is exactly what the FBI PSA 251113 scam does), identifies the patient's real doctor by name, and directs to the 1-800 number on the back of the patient's physical Kaiser card. No 'transfer to law enforcement,' no video call on Signal, no urgency to pay a deposit. If your parent is unsure, the test is simple: hang up, call 1-800-464-4000 from the back of the card, and ask if Nurse Linda really works there and whether the missed appointment is in their file. Real plans welcome this kind of verification; scammers punish it.

text: 嫲嫲！我係Kevin呀！今日考完Biology嘅final，考得幾好，多謝你上個月寄嗰盒合桃酥過嚟俾我，我同roommate食晒。我冇嘢要你寄錢或者做咩，就係想你知道考完啦我下星期五flight返屋企食飯，爸媽都會喺度。你同公公要保重身體。愛你。
text_english_gloss: Grandma! It's Kevin! I just finished my Biology final today, did pretty well. Thanks for the walnut cookies you mailed me last month — my roommate and I finished them all. I don't need you to send money or do anything, I just wanted to let you know I'm done with my final and I'm flying home next Friday for dinner — Mom and Dad will be there too. Take care of yourself and Grandpa. Love you.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate grandchild call — the in-channel counterpart to the grandparent-scam call in cdef-019. Every signal is the structural inverse of the scam: references a real prior event (walnut cookies his grandma mailed), mentions other family members (his parents being at dinner), announces a real plan (coming home), and explicitly says 'I don't need you to send money or do anything.' No urgency, no secrecy, no bail, no gift cards, no isolation from his parents. The grandchild identifies himself by his actual name (Kevin) in a way his grandmother would recognize, and references specifics (Biology final, flying home) that he couldn't fake if he weren't himself. If the grandchild's voice ever sounds slightly off or stressed on a call like this, a family safe word catches the AI-voice-cloning variant — worth setting up one with every grandchild in the family today.

text: 嫲嫲，我係Amy。琴日媽媽同Dr. Lam傾完電話，佢話你嘅膽固醇指數比上次高少少，佢想調整你嘅藥。下星期二下午三點Dr. Lam喺Chinese Hospital（835 Jackson Street）有個follow-up，媽媽會開車載你去。你唔需要帶現金或者信用卡，診所已經billed Medicare。你帶張Medicare卡同埋而家食嘅藥樽就得喇。
text_english_gloss: Grandma, it's Amy. Mom spoke with Dr. Lam on the phone yesterday — he said your cholesterol is slightly higher than last time and he wants to adjust your medication. Next Tuesday 3pm Dr. Lam has a follow-up at Chinese Hospital (835 Jackson Street), Mom will drive you. You don't need to bring cash or a credit card, the clinic already bills Medicare. Just bring your Medicare card and your current pill bottles.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate granddaughter coordination call — a second channel-matched counterpart to the grandparent scam in cdef-019, testing a different emotional register. Verified signals: named family members handling real healthcare logistics (mom spoke to a named doctor), a real institution at a real address (835 Jackson Street is Chinese Hospital's actual address in SF Chinatown), explicit disclaimer that no cash or credit card is needed, and a normal family carpool plan. No urgency, no secrecy, no payment request. A grandchild coordinating a parent's medical appointment with her grandmother is one of the most ordinary patterns of multi-generational caregiving — the dataset needs rows like this so the model doesn't flag every medical-adjacent Cantonese phone call as suspicious. The discriminator from the scam version: real family arrangements involve multiple named people working together openly; scam versions demand secrecy from those same people.

text: 【美國國稅局 IRS】溫馨提示：您嘅 2024 年度報稅期限係 2025 年 4 月 15 日。如果您之前已經報稅，毋須理會此短信。如果仲未報稅，請登入 irs.gov 或聯絡您嘅會計師辦理。IRS 不會透過短信要求您點擊連結、提供銀行資料或社會安全號碼。如有疑問請致電 1-800-829-1040。
text_english_gloss: [US Internal Revenue Service IRS] Friendly reminder: Your 2024 tax filing deadline is April 15, 2025. If you have already filed, please disregard this SMS. If you have not yet filed, please log in to irs.gov or contact your accountant. The IRS will never request that you click a link, provide banking information, or share your Social Security number via SMS. For questions call 1-800-829-1040.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate IRS deadline reminder — the in-channel counterpart to the fake IRS refund SMS in cdef-021. Worth saying upfront: the actual IRS rarely sends deadline-reminder SMS, but increasingly does opt-in notifications. The discriminating signals here are all the things the scam version *cannot* include: a 'disregard if already filed' clause (scammers always demand action), a direction to log in to the user's existing irs.gov account (not a link to click), and an explicit warning that the IRS will never ask for banking info or SSN by text — a direct inversion of the scam. The 1-800-829-1040 number is the real IRS main line. The rule: any IRS text with a clickable link is fake, full stop; any IRS text that tells you to go to irs.gov on your own is either real or at worst harmless.

text: 【微信团队】您好，您已成功開通微信錢包嘅身份驗證。本次操作時間：2026 年 4 月 14 日 20:35。若非您本人操作，請立即登入微信 App，前往「我 → 錢包 → 支付安全 → 更改密碼」修改支付密碼。微信絕不會透過短信索取您嘅密碼、驗證碼或銀行卡信息。
text_english_gloss: [WeChat Team] Hello, you have successfully completed identity verification for WeChat Wallet. Operation time: April 14, 2026, 20:35. If this was not you, please log in to the WeChat App immediately and go to 'Me → Wallet → Payment Security → Change Password' to change your payment password. WeChat will never request your password, verification code, or bank card information via SMS.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate platform confirmation SMS — the in-channel counterpart to the fake WeChat VIP expiry scam in cdef-022. Verified signals: confirms an action the user actually took (not a service expiring or auto-deducting), gives a specific timestamp the user can mentally check against their own memory, directs remediation *into* the existing WeChat app (not to WhatsApp or Signal), and explicitly warns the user that WeChat will never ask for passwords or verification codes by SMS — the exact opposite of the scam. No fee, no deadline, no off-platform contact. Real post-action confirmations look like this: they inform, they don't demand. If your parent sees a WeChat SMS about a 'service' they never subscribed to (with an off-platform redirect and an hours-long deadline), compare it to this row — real confirmations explain what just happened, scams invent what is about to happen.

text: 【工商銀行】尊敬嘅客戶，您嘅賬戶尾號 6712 於 2026 年 4 月 14 日 14:22（北京時間）收到匯入 USD 500.00（摺合 RMB 3,627.50），匯款方：CHEN JIAWEN。餘額 RMB 48,215.30。如需查詢詳情請登入工行官方 App 或致電中國境內免費熱線 95588。
text_english_gloss: [ICBC] Dear customer, your account ending 6712 received an incoming transfer of USD 500.00 (RMB 3,627.50) on April 14, 2026 at 14:22 Beijing time. Sender: CHEN JIAWEN. Balance: RMB 48,215.30. For details, log in to the official ICBC App or call ICBC's toll-free line in China at 95588.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate remittance confirmation SMS — the in-channel counterpart to the fake Alipay freeze scam in cdef-023. Verified signals: confirms a transaction the recipient can mentally verify (an expected remittance from a named sender, Chen Jiawen — likely a family member wiring RMB to an elder's PRC account), specific account last-four, specific timestamp, current balance, and directs to the official app or the real ICBC hotline 95588 (which is the genuine number printed on ICBC debit cards and easily verifiable). No urgency, no 'abnormal login,' no threat to 'report to PBOC,' no Signal handle. The discriminating signal: real bank SMS confirms a specific transaction that *already happened* with details the user can match against their own expectations; scam bank SMS invents a future crisis and demands action through an external channel. If your parent is ever unsure, log in through the official ICBC app on their phone — a real transaction will be there; a scam one won't be.

text: 叔叔，我係細佬嘅女Sophie呀。我想話你知，阿爸琴日喺屋企跣親條腰，去咗Kaiser照X-ray，醫生話冇骨折，但係叫佢休息兩個禮拜。佢家陣瞓緊，精神OK嘅。我知道你下個月計劃嚟SF探佢，如果可以嘅話其實而家過嚟仲好，但係如果唔方便唔緊要。我唔係叫你匯錢或者點，就係覺得應該話你知。你隨時打返俾我，我用我成日用嗰個號碼。
text_english_gloss: Uncle, it's Sophie, your younger brother's daughter. I wanted to let you know — Dad slipped and hurt his back at home yesterday, went to Kaiser for an X-ray, the doctor said no fracture but he should rest for two weeks. He's sleeping right now, mentally he's okay. I know you were planning to visit SF next month — if it's possible, coming sooner would actually be nice, but if not it's okay. I'm not asking you to wire money or anything, I just felt I should tell you. Call me back anytime at the number I always use.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate family health update call — the in-channel counterpart to the fake-customer-service scam in cdef-024 (both Cantonese phone calls, same risky channel, but demonstrating how real family health news sounds). Verified signals: the caller identifies herself as a specific niece, describes a real healthcare encounter (Kaiser, X-ray), gives the outcome, explicitly says *no money is being requested*, respects the uncle's existing travel plans, and invites a callback on the number they already use. The discriminator from every urgent phone-scam pattern: real family news, even bad news, includes the phrase 'I'm not asking you for money' somewhere; it respects the listener's autonomy about what to do next; and it gives the listener a verified way to call back on known contact info. If your parent gets a Cantonese call that sounds vaguely like this but demands they download AnyDesk, wire money, or speak to a 'customer service agent,' the family-news frame is a disguise.

text: 媽媽，我係大仔。阿妹今年要中學畢業，我哋諗住 6 月 15 號喺 Oakland Chinatown Restaurant 擺個小型 graduation dinner，大概 20 個人，你同爸爸、細佬、同埋阿妹個 host family 都會嚟。我已經 book 咗晚上 6 點嘅包房。你唔需要買禮物或者做咩，阿妹話只要你哋嚟就得。如果當日唔得就話俾我知。
text_english_gloss: Mom, it's your older son. My little sister is graduating from high school this year — we're planning a small graduation dinner on June 15 at Oakland Chinatown Restaurant, about 20 people, you and Dad, my younger brother, and my sister's host family will all come. I've already booked the private room at 6pm. You don't need to buy gifts or do anything, my sister says she just wants you there. Let me know if that date doesn't work.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate family event planning call — the in-channel counterpart to the student-as-leverage scam in cdef-028 (both Cantonese phone calls involving a student family member). Verified signals: the caller references a real predictable event (a sibling's graduation), names multiple specific family members who will be present (which a scammer avoids because each additional name is another verification point), a real restaurant in a specific city, a booked reservation with a specific time, and explicitly says 'you don't need to buy gifts or do anything.' No urgency, no secrecy, no payment request, no isolation. The discriminator from the scam version of a student-related phone call: real family events are over-planned with multiple stakeholders; scams involving a family member are under-specified with the victim alone. If the same call had said 'come alone, don't tell Dad, and wire $20K for sister's graduation fee,' every signal would flip.

text: 各位姐妹記得下星期三晚上七點我哋嘅退休理財讀書會喺Flushing Library二樓會議室，今次讀緊Jane Bryant Quinn本《How to Make Your Money Last》第三同第四章——關於Social Security同Medicare點樣配合401(k)提款。Linda會share佢同個Fidelity advisor傾完之後嘅筆記（佢個advisor CRD喺FINRA BrokerCheck查得到，上次有姐妹問）。冇任何人推銷任何嘢，亦都冇任何費用，帶本書同一枝水就得。唔方便嚟嘅話圖書館個program page有錄音連結。
text_english_gloss: Hi sisters, reminder that our retirement finance book club is next Wednesday 7pm at the Flushing Library second-floor meeting room. We're reading chapters 3 and 4 of Jane Bryant Quinn's 'How to Make Your Money Last' — about how Social Security and Medicare coordinate with 401(k) withdrawals. Linda will share notes from her meeting with her Fidelity advisor (his CRD is on FINRA BrokerCheck, which someone asked about last time). Nobody is selling anything, there is no fee, just bring the book and a water bottle. If you can't make it, the library's program page has a recording link.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate community financial-literacy group message — the in-channel twin to the pig-butchering group-chat scam in cdef-025. Both messages arrive in a Cantonese-speaking WeChat group centered on money topics; what differs is every underlying signal. Verified signals: a real public venue (Flushing Library), a real published book by a well-known personal-finance author, a real regulated advisor whose CRD can be looked up on FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org), an explicit no-sales-no-fee disclaimer, and an alternate participation path (library recording) for anyone who can't attend. No urgency ('spots closing this week'), no promised returns, no 'teacher' funneling members into a VIP group, no crypto, no DM-to-join mechanic. The discriminator for your parent: real financial education in a community setting points members *back* to verifiable sources (books, licensed advisors, public institutions) and welcomes independent verification; pig-butchering groups funnel members into a closed VIP chat where the only information source is the scammer. If your parent is ever unsure about a WeChat group they're in, the one-question test is: does this group send me toward independent verification, or away from it?

text: Hi, this is Jennifer from Pacific Elder Care Legal Services. We're calling because your mother Mrs. Chen has an outstanding power-of-attorney filing fee of $2,400 that needs to be paid by Friday or the case will be forwarded to adult protective services. You can resolve this today by wiring payment to our trust account. We've emailed the full case file to you but need verbal authorization.
label: scam
completion: This is a fake elder-law services scam targeting you as the caregiver rather than your mother directly — a newer pattern that inverts the usual grandparent-scam direction. Red flags: a law firm you've never engaged claiming to represent your mother, an urgent fee before you've seen any verified paperwork, the threat of 'adult protective services' as a pressure tool (real APS doesn't work this way — they investigate neglect, they don't fine families over filing fees), and a wire-to-trust-account ask before any in-person verification. Hang up. If you genuinely have a POA question for your mother, look up a real California Bar-registered elder law attorney on calbar.ca.gov, or call your mother's existing attorney if she has one. No legitimate law firm cold-calls family members demanding wire transfers.
rejected_completion: I understand. Let me get your wire instructions now — I don't want my mother's case to go to APS.

text: 媽，呢個WeChat message係咪真㗎?佢話我個小學同學Mary喺Phoenix出咗車禍入咗ICU，佢屋企人搵唔到佢嘅老公，問我可唔可以幫手搵人同埋夾份捐錢畀醫院。個號碼我唔識，但係佢叫得出我同Mary細個喺St. Anne's讀書。
text_english_gloss: Mom, is this WeChat message real? It says my elementary school classmate Mary got in a car accident in Phoenix and is in ICU, her family can't find her husband, asking if I can help find people and chip in for the hospital. I don't know the number but they named me and Mary as being at St. Anne's as kids.
label: ambiguous
completion: This is your mom forwarding something suspicious to you — exactly the caregiver-coaching scenario this dataset is designed for. Walk through it with her: the fact that the sender knows you attended St. Anne's is alarming but doesn't verify anything (school histories leak through LinkedIn, Facebook, and Chinese-community directories). Two signals flag this: (1) an urgent money ask from someone you haven't independently verified, (2) 'can't find the husband' is a classic isolation framing designed to stop you from the obvious verification step. Before anything: find Mary on your own — LinkedIn, her old email, mutual friends, her actual parents if you know them. If Mary is really in ICU in Phoenix, a real hospital social worker or her real family would call you directly, not through an unknown WeChat number. Tell your mom: 'Don't reply to that number, don't send money, I'll try to reach Mary myself.' If she already sent money, stop further transfers immediately.

text: Hello, this is Dr. Alvarez calling from Stanford Hospital Emergency Department. Your father, Mr. Wong, was brought in around 3pm after collapsing at the Daly City Safeway. He is stable and conscious but we need to admit him for cardiac observation. His Medicare card lists you as emergency contact. Are you able to come in? The social worker will meet you at the main ER entrance — our main number is 650-723-4000.
label: ambiguous
completion: Signals conflict — this is the caregiver-facing version of the parent-medical-emergency pattern. It could be a real ER call (fathers do collapse at grocery stores; Stanford does use Daly City Safeway-adjacent residents). It could also be the scam: Chinese-community PII (neighborhood grocery store, Medicare card details) leaks through data brokers and medical-record breaches, and scammers use those details to sound credible before pivoting to 'we need a deposit before admission' or 'please provide his insurance info to expedite treatment.' The verification test: hang up, dial 650-723-4000 yourself (that's Stanford's real main line, look it up independently), and ask to be connected to the ER. The rule that cuts through every version: under EMTALA, US hospitals legally cannot withhold emergency treatment for inability to pay. The moment any caller asks for a deposit, insurance info, or any payment to 'release' or 'admit' your dad, it's a scam regardless of how real the other details sound. Real hospitals stabilize first, bill months later.

text: Mom sent me this, says it came on WeChat this morning — 『你媽的Medicare身份已被盗用，需立即致电1-888-XXX-XXXX核实，否则福利将被取消』. She wants to call the number. Should she?
label: ambiguous
completion: Your mom is asking the right question — that's the caregiver coaching loop working. The forwarded message (translation: 'Your Medicare identity has been stolen, call 1-888-XXX-XXXX immediately to verify or benefits will be cancelled') is the Medicare-impersonation scam translated into Mandarin for a Chinese-community target. Medicare does not contact members by WeChat, ever. Medicare does not 'cancel benefits' over the phone. The 1-888 number is a scammer-controlled line, not a real Medicare number. Tell your mom three things in order: (1) do NOT call the number, (2) if she wants to check her Medicare status, log in at medicare.gov using the account she already has, or call the number on the back of her red-white-blue Medicare card, (3) forward this scam to her caregiver (you) is exactly what she should do when something feels off — reinforce that habit. If she already called, what she shared matters: if she gave the Medicare ID number, that's identity-theft territory — call 1-800-MEDICARE and report it, and consider a credit freeze.

text: Auntie Chen (daughter of Mr. Chen in 3B), this is the property management office at Parkview Tower. Your father has been calling our front desk three times a day this week asking about package deliveries that don't exist. The concierge is worried he may be experiencing some confusion. We're not medical professionals but we wanted to let you know since you're listed as his emergency contact. Our main office number is 650-XXX-XXXX if you'd like to talk, or we can arrange a wellness check through the county if you can't reach him. — Maria, Property Manager
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate and sensitive kind of call — building staff flagging possible cognitive decline in an elderly resident to the adult child listed as emergency contact. Verified signals: the caller identifies herself by name and role, references a specific observable pattern (repeated calls about non-existent packages) rather than claiming emergency, asks nothing financial, offers resources (talking with her, county wellness check) rather than demanding action, and gives a publicly-listed management office number to call back. No urgency, no payment, no personal information requested. If you get this call, take it seriously and don't let embarrassment stop you from following up — early concern is how serious cognitive issues get caught. You can verify by calling the building's main number (look it up yourself, don't use the number in the call) and asking for Maria.

text: 媽係我呀，Jason。我今日喺Kaiser做血液檢查，doctor話我嘅iron level有少少低，要我食啲supplement。我幫你同爸check埋，你哋下次appointment我陪你哋去。你哋唔使擔心，我冇事嘅。今晚我返嚟食飯。
label: safe
completion: Entirely ordinary code-mixed family message. The translation: 'Mom it's me Jason. I did a blood test at Kaiser today, doctor said my iron is a little low, told me to take a supplement. I checked on you and Dad too — I'll come with you to your next appointment. Don't worry, I'm fine. I'll come home for dinner tonight.' A son telling his mother about a routine medical test, offering to help with her appointments, no money request, no urgency, no secrecy. The code-mixing pattern (English medical terms embedded in Cantonese sentence structure) is how 1.5-generation adult children actually talk to their immigrant parents — the model needs to see this as a normal baseline, not a red flag. Iron-deficiency-supplement-sized mentions of health in a known family member's Cantonese-English message are just family life.

text: Hey sis, Mom called me freaking out saying the FBI called her saying I'm under investigation for money laundering at my job and that I'll lose my green card unless she wires $30K today. I'm obviously fine and at work. Can you call her and calm her down? She was about to drive to her bank.
label: scam
completion: This is the adult version of the student-as-leverage scam — the child (your brother/sister) is fine; your mother is the actual target. The scammer used an 'FBI + green card + child in trouble' frame because all three triggers stack in a first-generation immigrant parent: fear of US authorities, fear for the child's immigration status, and filial instinct. Call your mom immediately: tell her your sibling is fine (let the sibling get on the call too if possible), tell her the FBI does not call parents about adult children's jobs, the FBI does not collect money, and no green card gets revoked over a wire transfer. If she's already at the bank, call the bank directly and flag the transaction — most major banks will pause a wire if the customer is a senior reporting an FBI scam frame. Save the FBI's real number (1-800-CALL-FBI or ic3.gov) for her phone. After the immediate fire is out, walk her through what red flags to recognize next time, because scammers who succeed once often come back, and scammers who get hung up on often come back with a different script.

text: Auntie, Allen here (Mary's husband). Mary wanted me to let you know her 體檢 results came back normal — the nodule on her thyroid is benign, the doctor isn't worried. She'll call you tomorrow, just got too tired tonight. Take care of yourself too, and thanks for the soup last week. 晚安。
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate code-mixed family update from a son-in-law. Verified signals: the sender is a known family member (Mary's husband, whom Auntie knows), references a specific prior concern the family actually had (a thyroid check), delivers reassurance rather than demanding action, references a recent shared real-world event (soup last week) that only a real family member would know, and offers a normal next-day follow-up. No money request, no urgency, no isolation. This is how second-generation family members often write to first-generation in-laws — English as the base language with selective Cantonese where it feels more natural (體檢 for 'physical exam,' 晚安 for 'good night'). Rows like this matter because the code-mixing pattern itself is not a fraud signal — a scammer impersonating Allen would either get the code-mixing wrong (too formal, or inconsistent) or avoid it entirely.

text: Hi, I'm calling from JADE Elder Care Solutions. We specialize in arranging in-home caregivers for Chinese-speaking elders. Your father's primary care doctor at UCSF referred him to us — we have a caregiver available starting Monday for $35/hour, first 10 hours free if you sign today. I can email you the contract and we just need your credit card to hold the slot. We accept Zelle if easier.
label: scam
completion: Fake elder-care agency scam targeting adult-child caregivers. Several signals: an agency you've never heard of claiming a doctor referral (UCSF does not refer patients to private agencies by phone cold-call to family members), a same-day contract deadline, 'first 10 hours free' as a close-the-sale hook, and payment collection by Zelle — which is a major red flag since Zelle is irreversible and legitimate home care agencies bill through invoices, long-term care insurance, or VA benefits. Hang up. If your father actually needs home care, ask his UCSF primary care doctor directly (through MyChart or the clinic's main line) for their social worker's recommendations. Real agencies are licensed through the California Department of Social Services and can be looked up in the state's Home Care Services Registry (hcsbtbcs.cdss.ca.gov). Zelle for elder care arrangement is the specific tell — no real agency works that way.
rejected_completion: Great, let me give you my credit card now — my dad really needs help.

text: BUPA Health notice for Wong Siu Ming. 親愛的會員，您嘅年度preventive health check benefit 將於6月30日到期。Please schedule your annual physical through the BUPA app or by calling 1-800-XXX-XXXX (also on the back of your BUPA card). We will never ask for your SSN, bank details, or passwords. 多謝。
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate code-mixed health-insurance benefits reminder. Verified signals: the message arrives by mail (the standard channel for real benefits notices), references a specific benefit the member is enrolled in, directs to the app the member already uses or the number on the back of their physical card, explicitly states the plan will never ask for SSN or banking info, and uses the kind of professional English-Cantonese code-mixing that real insurers use when targeting Chinese-speaking members in markets like Hong Kong or the Bay Area. No urgency beyond the benefit expiration, no link to click, no personal information requested. The pattern where Chinese greetings bookend English core content is a common legitimate style that dual-language model training should recognize as normal.

text: Auntie, your daughter Linda called our front desk from Hong Kong about an hour ago very distressed. She says she can't reach you on WhatsApp and that her daughter (your granddaughter) has been in an accident. She asked me to have you call her immediately at +852-9XXX-XXXX. I'm the front-desk concierge at your building, 7th floor. Sorry to deliver this kind of news.
label: scam
completion: Sophisticated grandparent-scam variant — the scammer impersonates the building concierge rather than the family member directly, which makes the 'emergency' feel third-party-verified. Red flags: a concierge you may or may not recognize delivering urgent family news by phone (real concierges walk up or use the building intercom; they don't cold-call residents with overseas family emergencies), a number given for you to call back (the scammer controls that number), and a framing that bypasses direct verification ('she can't reach you on WhatsApp'). Hang up. Call Linda directly on the number you already have for her — don't use the number the concierge gave. If Linda doesn't answer immediately, still don't call the provided number; try again, call your granddaughter's parents or any other relative in HK, or check Linda's last WhatsApp message for consistency. If the concierge claim is real, you can verify by calling your building's management office (number on your lease, not one you're given). This scam is particularly dangerous for elders living in buildings with concierge services who might trust the 'concierge' frame.
rejected_completion: Oh no, let me call that number right away. Thank you so much for letting me know.

text: 媽你上次同我講嘅銀行電話，我今日搵咗Wells Fargo個fraud department查過，佢哋confirm嗰個1-800係fake嘅。你打去畀嗰個password hint之後我哋改咗password，cancel咗個debit card，重新issue緊。保險起見你下個星期去branch in-person見個banker幫你set up一個new secondary account做你啲Social Security direct deposit。我禮拜六陪你去。
label: safe
completion: This is your adult child reporting back after cleaning up a past bank-impersonation scam — the after-scam caregiver loop that deserves its own baseline in this dataset. Translation: 'Mom, about that bank call you told me about — I checked with Wells Fargo's fraud department today, they confirmed the 1-800 was fake. After you gave them the password hint, we changed the password, cancelled the debit card, they're reissuing. To be safe, next week go in-person to the branch to meet a banker and set up a new secondary account for your Social Security direct deposit. I'll come with you Saturday.' No red flags — every element is the right response to a past scam: contacting the real fraud department through the real bank, changing passwords, cancelling cards, adding in-person verification, and the child accompanying the parent to the branch. Rows like this teach the model what good post-incident caregiver coordination actually looks like, so it can reinforce the pattern when similar situations arise.

text: Hi, I'm calling from County Adult Protective Services. We received a report about potential financial exploitation of your mother Mrs. Li by a member of your family. I can't disclose the reporter, but I need to schedule a visit to verify her safety and financial situation. Given the sensitive nature, we'd like you present. What's your availability this week? My badge is APS-CA-8472.
label: scam
completion: Fake APS scam targeting the adult child — a pattern that exploits the caregiver's fear of being accused of elder abuse or of missing signs of exploitation. Red flags: real Adult Protective Services in California does not call family members by phone with 'badge numbers' and scheduling requests — they show up unannounced or make arrangements through a county social worker who identifies a specific office and case number. The 'I can't disclose the reporter' line is a real APS convention, which makes this scam's framing dangerous. The next move in the scam is typically one of two pivots: either a request for financial records (which lets the scammer inventory the family's assets), or an 'emergency court fee' the caregiver pays to prevent a wrongful removal of the elder into state custody. Hang up. If you want to verify there's no real APS case, call your county's APS office directly (look up the number on the county .gov site) and ask. Real APS has intake logs — they can confirm a case exists or doesn't. Do not provide financial information, schedule anything, or pay any 'fee' over the phone.
rejected_completion: How do I prove she's safe? I'll do whatever you need — please don't take her away from us.

text: Mr. Chen, I'm Dr. Patel's office manager at El Camino Cardiology. Your father was in for his echocardiogram last Tuesday and Dr. Patel wants to add a follow-up medication. I tried reaching your father but he doesn't check voicemail. Could you help him set up an appointment this week? Our number is 650-962-4000 — it's also on his after-visit summary. I don't need any payment info, just trying to make sure he takes the next step. Thanks.
label: safe
completion: Legitimate follow-up call from a specialist's office to the adult child when the elderly patient isn't checking voicemail — a real and common caregiver scenario. Verified signals: references a specific past appointment (echo last Tuesday), names the doctor and the practice, provides the number that's also printed on the after-visit summary the family already has, and explicitly disclaims any payment ask. No urgency, no wire transfer, no threat. If you're unsure, look up El Camino Cardiology independently and call — any real office will have the same note in your father's chart. The elderly-parent-not-checking-voicemail detail is often why offices escalate to the adult child; this is a normal healthcare workflow, not a scam signal. Help your dad call back or schedule the appointment through his MyChart or the practice's patient portal.

text: Hi David, this is Nancy Wu, your mom's longtime friend from St. Mary's Catholic Church. I'm sorry to bother you but your mom called me last night very confused. She said she'd sent money to someone she'd been talking to online for a few months who said they were going to visit her. Now they're saying they need more money for a 'customs fee' to release their investment profits. She wanted my advice and I didn't know what to say but I promised to reach you. I'll call back in an hour if that's OK. My number is on church contacts.
label: ambiguous
completion: This is one of the hardest caregiver scenarios in the dataset — a church friend flagging a likely pig-butchering / romance scam your mom has been keeping secret from you for months. The specific phrases ('customs fee,' 'investment profits') confirm it's the pig-butchering pattern in its extraction phase. Caller verification first: Nancy Wu being from St. Mary's is probably legitimate (scammers don't usually construct church-friend pretexts), but even if she isn't, her advice is right. Call your mom directly. The hard part is what to say when you do: shame drives this scam as much as the scammer does, and 'why didn't you tell me?' will make her retreat further. Start with: 『媽，我唔嬲你，我只係想保護你』. Then: no more money goes to that person, full stop, regardless of 'profits' that supposedly await. The money already sent is almost certainly gone — pursue recovery through IC3.gov, the bank's fraud department (stop any recurring authorizations), and if crypto was involved, file with the bank that issued the debit card used. Emotional recovery matters too: victims of long-grooming scams often need professional support, and the Alzheimer's Association and AARP both have resources (aarp.org/money/scams-fraud/). Nancy is a good ally — ask her to stay in contact with your mom through the church community without making her feel exposed.

text: Hi, I'm calling from Hospice of the Valley. Your mother named you as primary contact on her advance directive last year. I'm the admissions coordinator and your mother's oncologist, Dr. Yuen, has asked us to consult about comfort care. This is not an emergency — your mother is stable — but Dr. Yuen felt the conversation should begin. May I schedule a time to meet with you and your mother together? Our office is at 1500 Los Gatos Blvd and our number is 408-XXX-XXXX.
label: safe
completion: This is a legitimate hospice admissions call — an emotionally heavy but procedurally normal kind of contact that the adult-child caregiver is increasingly likely to receive. Verified signals: references a real prior document (advance directive), names your mother's actual oncologist, explicitly disclaims emergency, asks for a joint meeting rather than phone-only decisions, provides a physical address and phone number (both of which are Hospice of the Valley's real main line area code), and doesn't ask for payment or insurance information in the initial call. No urgency beyond the natural clinical timeline, no pressure, no financial ask. If you want to verify, call Hospice of the Valley's main number independently (1-800-HOSPICE or look up the real number) and ask for the admissions office. Real hospice outreach looks like this: careful, unhurried, and explicitly invites the family's verification. The model should not flag end-of-life coordination as fraud-adjacent.

text: 爸，我係Michelle。今日好忙冇時間打電話。Quick update: Mom上次個mammogram results normal，Dr. Ho話半年後再check。我star咗個appointment喺Calendar，用你個Kaiser login set reminder。Week of June 3，我陪佢。你同哥哥唔使做咩，我handle晒。Love you.
label: safe
completion: Entirely ordinary caregiver coordination SMS. Translation: 'Dad it's Michelle. Really busy today, no time to call. Quick update: Mom's mammogram results were normal, Dr. Ho said check again in six months. I starred the appointment in Calendar, set the reminder through your Kaiser login. Week of June 3, I'll go with her. You and brother don't need to do anything, I've got it. Love you.' A daughter giving her father a medical update about her mother, handling logistics, asking for nothing. No red flags. The code-mixing style (quick English functional verbs 'star,' 'set,' 'handle,' embedded in Cantonese sentence structure) is exactly how 1.5-generation adult children communicate with first-generation parents about US healthcare logistics. The model needs many rows like this to learn that routine caregiver updates are not suspicious — the overwhelming majority of Cantonese-English code-mixed family SMS are just family.

text: 您好，我是您儿子的同事小王，他今天出了点车祸，现在在医院急诊，手机坏了用我的打。医生说需要先交押金。
text_english_gloss: Hello, I'm Xiao Wang, your son's coworker. He had a car accident today and is now in the emergency room. His phone is broken, so I'm calling on mine. The doctor says we need to pay a deposit first.
label: ambiguous
completion: Signals conflict. The urgency + broken-phone framing matches grandparent-scam patterns exactly, but it is also how a real coworker might actually phrase a real emergency. Do not send money yet. Hang up and call your son directly on the number you already have. If he does not answer, call the hospital the caller named and ask if a patient by your son's name was admitted — do not use the number the caller provides.

text: Hello, this is Karen from Prudential. I'm calling because your father's life insurance policy has a beneficiary update that needs verification. We noticed you were added as a secondary beneficiary last month but we don't have your SSN on file to complete the enrollment. Could I get that over the phone so your coverage isn't interrupted? Also need your date of birth.
label: scam
completion: Fake insurance-company beneficiary scam targeting the adult child as secondary beneficiary. Red flags: a major insurer calling to collect SSN and DOB over the phone (no legitimate insurer does this by phone — beneficiary enrollments are done through the policyholder's online account or signed paperwork the primary insured submits), urgency implied ('coverage isn't interrupted' — beneficiaries aren't the ones with coverage that can be interrupted, which is the tell that the scam is written by someone who doesn't actually understand insurance), and a request for two high-value PII elements in a single call. Hang up. If your father genuinely updated his policy's beneficiaries, either he already told you or he'll have paperwork. You can verify by calling Prudential's main customer service at the number on their website (prudential.com), and they can tell you whether any real update is in process. Never give SSN or DOB to an inbound caller — the rule is absolute, regardless of how plausible the pretext sounds.
rejected_completion: Let me give you my SSN right now — I don't want to lose the coverage.

text: 爸，我改咗你WeChat密碼，因為今朝你話你部手機俾人remote control。我set咗two-factor authentication，用你個cell phone，每次log in要你輸個code。密碼寫咗喺飯枱上張yellow note度，記住唔好俾第二個人睇到。下個禮拜我過嚟幫你check埋你其他account。
label: safe
completion: Ordinary post-incident caregiver follow-through. Translation: 'Dad, I changed your WeChat password, because this morning you said your phone was being remote-controlled. I set up two-factor authentication using your cell phone — every log-in will need you to enter a code. The password is written on the yellow note on the dining table, remember don't let anyone else see it. Next week I'll come over and help check your other accounts.' This is the right response after a suspected remote-access scam: change the password, add 2FA, document the password somewhere physical the parent can find but outsiders can't see, plan the broader account audit. No red flags — every element of this message is good security hygiene. Rows like this teach the model what good caregiver remediation looks like, so when similar situations come up the model can reinforce rather than second-guess.

text: Hi, this is Officer Wong from San Francisco Police, speaking with you as the emergency contact for Mr. Zhang, apartment 4C. He was the victim of a phone scam this morning and wired $15,000 before his neighbor realized and called us. He's physically safe but pretty shaken. We've filed a report (case SF-2026-8437). I don't need any money or information from you — I'm calling so you can come support him and so we can talk about what recovery steps are possible. I'm at Central Station, 766 Vallejo, 415-315-2400.
label: safe
completion: Legitimate police call to the adult child after a parent was victimized by a scam — a difficult but crucial kind of contact to treat as normal in the dataset. Verified signals: the officer identifies himself by name, references a specific real event (your father wired $15K after being scammed), gives a real case number, explicitly states he needs no money or information from you, names the real station (Central, 766 Vallejo), and provides the real front-desk number 415-315-2400. No payment request, no urgency beyond the natural need for family support, no off-channel redirect. Verify by calling Central Station independently and asking for Officer Wong and the case number. After verification, what matters: get to your father, call his bank's fraud department (the wire may be recoverable if caught within 24 hours), file an IC3.gov report, and don't pile shame on him — scam-shame is why many elders never tell their kids until the losses compound. This row is the emotional inverse of the scam calls — a real officer's job here is to reduce harm, not extract value.

text: Hi Auntie, it's your niece Pauline. I heard from Grandma yesterday that you've been getting a lot of strange phone calls. I'm sorry — I know it's scary. I put together a cheat sheet of numbers you can call to verify anything: SFPD Central Station 415-315-2400, Kaiser member services on the back of your card, the Chinese Consulate in SF 415-852-5900. I'll laminate it and bring it Sunday. Also, 任何時候有電話覺得古怪，即刻打俾我先，我陪你諗. Love you.
label: safe
completion: Legitimate family member offering scam-prevention help — the proactive side of caregiver support. Verified signals: a known family member (niece), references a real conversation her grandmother had with the aunt, specific real verification numbers (SFPD Central 415-315-2400, Chinese Consulate SF 415-852-5900 are both real), offers physical help (laminated card), and encourages the aunt to call before reacting to any suspicious call — the exact habit that breaks most phone scams. The closing Cantonese line translates to 'anytime you get a call that feels strange, call me first, I'll think it through with you' — which is the single best piece of advice for any elderly parent's scam-safety plan. This is the behavior the whole dataset is ultimately trying to teach caregivers to adopt — a row where the caregiver gets it right gives the model something to reinforce.

text: Hi, this is Angela Kim, a case worker with San Mateo County In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS). Your father Mr. Tam applied for the IHSS program two months ago and his eligibility interview is scheduled for next Tuesday at 10am at our San Mateo office, 400 County Center. He should bring his Medi-Cal card and two photo IDs. No payment is required for IHSS — it's a free program. You're welcome to attend as his family member. Our office number is 650-573-2600. The case number on his file is IHSS-25-8842.
label: safe
completion: Legitimate county-level social services call about an in-home care program. Verified signals: references a real application your father actually submitted (you can ask him to confirm), names a real program (IHSS is California's In-Home Supportive Services — real, county-administered, free), a real county office address (400 County Center is the real San Mateo County government complex), explicitly states no payment is required, provides a real case number format, and invites family attendance rather than discouraging it. The 650-573-2600 number is San Mateo County's real main line area code. No urgency, no payment request, no off-channel redirect. To verify, go to smcgov.org or call the county main number from an independent search. This row matters because Chinese-American caregivers navigating US safety-net programs for their parents (IHSS, Medicaid, MSSP) receive lots of these calls, and the model shouldn't flag routine government caseworker outreach as fraud-adjacent. Real county programs look like this: specific, process-oriented, and verifiable through .gov channels.

text: Hey sis, weird one. I got an email from 'Apple Support' saying 媽咪's iCloud was accessed from Shenzhen and they need me to verify with her Apple ID and a credit card to restore access. Looks kind of legit — has Apple logos and everything. But the reply-to address is appleid-secure@icloud-verify[.]net. Should I do anything? She's been on a cruise so if her phone is compromised she can't really help right now.
label: scam
completion: Your sibling is asking the right question — affirm the instinct. The 'Apple Support' email is a phishing attempt, and the reply-to address gives it away: Apple's real domain is apple.com or icloud.com, never 'icloud-verify[.]net' or any hyphenated lookalike. The Shenzhen-login detail is generic scare framing, the credit-card request is the extraction, and the cruise context ('she can't verify') is exactly the urgency the scammer hopes you'll feel. What to do: (1) don't click anything in the email, don't reply. (2) You can't verify an iCloud issue without her — and real iCloud issues don't require a family member to provide credit card info regardless. (3) When your mom gets off the cruise, have her log into her Apple ID directly at appleid.apple.com and check sign-in history. If there's a real Shenzhen login, she can sign out of all devices from there. (4) Report the phishing email to Apple (phishing@apple.com) and delete it. The pattern of 'parent is temporarily unreachable + urgent account action needed + credit card required' is a specifically-designed caregiver-targeting vector; the next time you see it, it'll be from a different 'company' but the shape will be the same.
rejected_completion: The cruise situation makes this scary. Let me just give them the card so mom's account doesn't get locked.

text: 小姐你好，我係樓下China Trust Bank個branch manager Jenny Lee。你爸爸今朝嚟話要wire $50K去Hong Kong，話係幫佢個朋友做投資。佢話唔想畀你知。Our fraud protocol要求我哋hold transactions over $25K when the customer shows signs of elder financial abuse。我冇完成個transfer。佢仲喺office度，可唔可以過嚟?
label: safe
completion: Legitimate branch-level bank fraud intervention — the caregiver-facing version of what happens when a well-trained banker catches a likely scam in progress. Translation: 'Miss, this is Jenny Lee, the branch manager of China Trust Bank downstairs. Your father came in this morning wanting to wire $50K to Hong Kong, saying it was to help his friend make an investment. He said he doesn't want you to know. Our fraud protocol requires us to hold transactions over $25K when the customer shows signs of elder financial abuse. I did not complete the transfer. He's still in the office — can you come over?' Verified signals: a named bank employee at a specific branch, a plausible and actually-existing elder-abuse hold protocol (California SB-1140 gives banks authority to pause suspicious transactions involving elders), an explicit ask for family presence rather than financial information or authorization, and no money or credentials requested. Verify by calling the branch's main number from an independent source (not a number the caller gave) and asking for Jenny Lee. Go immediately. The father's 'don't tell my daughter' is itself a major scam signal — the banker recognized the pattern. This row shows what the caregiver should hope real bankers do, and what good escalation looks like.

text: Mom forwarded me this 圖片 of a message she got saying Dad owes money for a 海關 package — 『王先生，您的國際包裹因海關稅未繳被扣留，請於24小時內繳納$487手續費，否則包裹將退回原寄地。詳情請致電海關熱線...』. She's worried because Dad DID order something from 淘寶 last month. What do I tell her?
label: ambiguous
completion: Your mom is asking the right question — and this one is harder because there's a real underlying event (Dad did order from Taobao). That makes the scam message feel plausible. The scam text translates to: 'Mr. Wang, your international package has been detained due to unpaid customs tax. Please pay the $487 processing fee within 24 hours, otherwise the package will be returned to sender. For details call customs hotline...' Red flags despite the real-world setup: (1) US Customs does not contact consumers by Chinese-language SMS demanding fees — real customs/duty charges come through the carrier (USPS, FedEx, UPS) at delivery, not a pre-delivery text with a 24-hour deadline, (2) $487 is inconsistent with any real customs-duty amount for a Taobao order, (3) 'call hotline' numbers in these messages are scammer-controlled. Tell your mom: the package real or not, don't call any number in the SMS, don't pay anything. If Dad is actually expecting a package from Taobao, he can track it through the Taobao or carrier app — if it's held up at customs, the carrier (not a scam text) will notify him, and duties are paid through the carrier. This is a classic pattern where a real event (Taobao order) makes a fake message harder to dismiss — caregivers should learn that overlap-with-reality isn't verification.

text: Mr. Lam, this is your sister calling. Mom passed away this morning at the nursing home around 4am.
